rationale: B wins because it finds the sharper live tension in the facts: "the company isn't yet saying how often they get it right" turns the missing reliability data into an actual enterprise IT story. A has usable bones, but "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" makes a market-wide claim from one Airtable repositioning. B is stricter about what can be pitched now, while A is a little too ready to send half-proved category and competitor angles into the street wearing a press badge.
gaps_in_A: "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" overstates the evidence. The update proves Airtable changed its pitch, not that the whole market moved.
"Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" is plausible but under-sourced. No competitor set, buyer comparison, or analyst map was supplied.
It misses the strongest negative-space angle: "agent-reliability data not disclosed". A asks about reliability later, but does not turn it into the obvious governance/trust story.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is premature. Several angles still need basic proof before matching reporters, especially valuation context, pricing, customer evidence, and reliability data.
gaps_in_B: "employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong" overreaches. The update does not say the agents make errors, lack approvals, or push cleanup onto employees.

"the prevailing belief this cuts against: that enterprise AI agents are now trustworthy enough" imports a market belief that was not in the update. The angle works, but that sentence is doing outside-the-record work.

"All four angles are blocked on the same gaps" is too blunt. The valuation angle needs valuation history and investor comment; the category angle needs positioning proof and an exec quote; the reliability angle needs error/approval data. Same family of holes, not the same hole.
